description: Width tiers for English Year 3 — 26 descriptors across Language, Literature and Literacy strands
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that satisfies the descriptor's command term. One context, one example — sufficient to demonstrate the concept or skill has been encountered. Anchored to the descriptor's verb, not to what is easy.
width_notes.typical_width: Full engagement with the descriptor as ACARA intended, grounded in the elaborations. Covers the scope and spirit of the descriptor across the range of examples named.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add contexts, phenomena or text types — not harder versions of the same thing. First Nations Australian directions included where elaborations indicate them. May reasonably infer beyond elaborations within the descriptor's territory.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are the primary source for typical_width and wider directions. They are examples of how the descriptor might be addressed, not a required sequence.

AC9E3LA01.minimum_width: Identify two collaborative language conventions and explain how they enable cooperation in group work.
AC9E3LA01.typical_width: Recognise and use collaborative language for initiating, inviting, responding and extending; understand turn-taking patterns, acknowledgement and body language as shared conventions that enable cooperation.
wider: Examine specific First Nations Australian cultural protocols and speaking/listening conventions — discussing how understanding different conventions enables respectful cooperation across communities
Compare how turn-taking conventions differ across formal group discussions versus casual conversations, and explain what changes between contexts
elaborations: recognising and using collaborative language in group and pair work; for example, initiating, inviting, responding and extending
understanding some First Nations Australian cultural protocols, cultural practices, specific speaking and listening conventions, and the significance of these practices

AC9E3LA02.minimum_width: Identify two modal verbs and explain the different degree of certainty each signals; identify one evaluative or emotional word choice and explain what opinion or feeling it expresses.
AC9E3LA02.typical_width: Explore how modal verbs indicate degrees of possibility and necessity; recognise how adverb, noun and verb choices present different evaluations of characters and events; build vocabulary for expressing emotions and opinions.
wider: Compare how the same character or event is described with different evaluative vocabulary in two versions of the same story, and discuss how word choice constructs point of view
Find examples of modal verbs in persuasive texts and analyse how modality is used to make claims sound more or less certain
elaborations: exploring how modal verbs; for example, 'must', 'might' and 'could', indicate degrees of possibility, probability or necessity
recognising how choice of adverbs, nouns and verbs present different evaluations of characters or events
exploring examples of language that demonstrate a range of emotions and positions, and building vocabulary for communicating these

AC9E3LA03.minimum_width: Describe the structure and at least two language features of one factual text type and explain how they serve the purpose.
AC9E3LA03.typical_width: Describe the typical structure and language features of factual recounts, autobiographies, procedures and reports; identify the stages of a basic argument (introduction, arguments, conclusion) and language features of each stage.
wider: Compare language features across two factual text types with different purposes, explaining why different features are needed for each purpose
Identify a text that mixes features from more than one type and discuss why the author made those choices
elaborations: identifying the stages of a basic argument such as introduction, argument one, argument 2 and conclusion
describing the typical text structure and language features of factual recounts, autobiographies, procedures and reports

AC9E3LA04.minimum_width: Identify at least two paragraphs in an informative text and explain what related information each groups together.
AC9E3LA04.typical_width: Recognise that informative paragraphs begin with a topic sentence and group related ideas; understand that narrative paragraphs vary in length and do not always follow a topic-sentence formula; examine models of well-constructed paragraphs.
wider: Compare two versions of the same information — one organised into paragraphs, one without — discussing the effect on the reader
Examine how a very short paragraph (even one sentence) is used for effect in a narrative, discussing what it achieves compared with a long paragraph
elaborations: recognising that longer informative texts are organised into paragraphs, which begin with a topic sentence
recognising that paragraphs in narrative texts vary in length and do not always follow a predictable formula
examining models of well-constructed paragraphs and identifying their features

AC9E3LA05.minimum_width: Identify two headings or subheadings and explain what purpose each serves; identify one hyperlink and explain what the hyperlink word signals.
AC9E3LA05.typical_width: Discuss the words used as headings and subheadings in print and digital information texts and chapter headings in narratives; examine hyperlink words in digital texts and explain how word choices signal where the link leads.
wider: Compare the words chosen as headings across two information texts on the same topic and discuss how different heading choices change reader expectation
Compare how navigation features differ between a print text and a digital text, discussing what each makes easy or difficult for the reader
elaborations: examining the words used as hyperlinks
discussing words used as headings and subheadings in digital and print information texts
discussing words used for chapter headings in narratives

AC9E3LA06.minimum_width: Identify the subject and verb in at least three clauses; identify one example of correct singular and one of correct plural subject-verb agreement.
AC9E3LA06.typical_width: Identify clauses by locating verbs and subjects; understand and apply subject-verb agreement for singular and plural subjects; recognise and correct agreement errors.
wider: Identify tricky agreement cases (collective nouns, compound subjects) and discuss why they are harder to get right

Limited width: subject-verb agreement is a precision convention that does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Extension goes toward harder agreement cases rather than contextual widening.
elaborations: identifying clauses in texts by locating verbs and the key words that link to the verbs
identifying that a singular subject has a singular verb and a plural subject has a plural verb

AC9E3LA07.minimum_width: Identify one doing verb, one saying verb and one sensing or relating verb in texts, explaining what type of process each represents.
AC9E3LA07.typical_width: Explore doing, saying, sensing (feeling/thinking) and relating verbs across narrative and informational texts — identifying types and explaining how each controls meaning in a clause differently.
wider: Compare the doing verbs in an action sequence versus a description in the same narrative, discussing what verb type choices reveal about pacing
Find sensing verbs in a narrative and discuss how they let readers understand characters' inner experience without direct statement
elaborations: exploring 'doing' and 'saying' verbs in narrative texts
exploring the use of sensing verbs and how they allow readers to understand what characters feel and think
exploring the use of relating verbs in constructing definitions and descriptions
identifying different types of verbs and the way they control meaning in a clause

AC9E3LA08.minimum_width: Identify present and past tense verbs in a text; correctly form the past tense of two regular and two irregular verbs.
AC9E3LA08.typical_width: Understand how tense anchors verbs in time; form regular past tense with '-ed' and recognise that irregular past tense forms change differently; apply tense knowledge in reading and writing.
wider: Examine why recounts use past tense while instructions use present tense — connecting tense choice to text purpose

Limited width: past tense irregular forms must be memorised and do not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Extension goes toward examining more irregular forms and exploring tense in different text types.
elaborations: learning how time is represented through the tense of a verb
learning that tenses for some verbs are formed by changing the word; for example, 'She caught.'

AC9E3LA09.minimum_width: Identify one piece of information an image adds that is not in the written text; identify one image feature (gaze, angle or distance) and explain the relationship it creates with the viewer.
AC9E3LA09.typical_width: Recognise how images extend meaning by adding information not in the words — including how character relationships are depicted through position and expression; understand how gaze, angle and distance construct a relationship between image and viewer.
wider: Compare two images of the same subject using different angles and distances, discussing how the choices change the viewer's relationship with the subject
Find examples in picture books or media where image choices position the viewer to feel sympathy or distance — analysing how technical choices create those effects
elaborations: recognising how the relationship between characters can be depicted in images through the positioning of characters
recognising how images construct a relationship with the viewer through direct gaze into the camera

AC9E3LA10.minimum_width: Identify and use three technical or topic-specific words from a learning area topic; identify one word with different meanings in different contexts.
AC9E3LA10.typical_width: Identify and use technical and topic-specific vocabulary across curriculum areas including metric length terms and narrative feature terms; recognise words that have different meanings in different contexts; extend vocabulary by adding prefixes and suffixes.
wider: Compare technical vocabulary from two different subject areas and discuss how each subject builds its own specialised vocabulary
Find examples of the same word used in an everyday context and a subject-specific context in the same week, and discuss how context signals which meaning is active
elaborations: identifying and using technical words to describe length, including metric units
identifying and using words to describe features of narratives
identifying words that have different meanings in different contexts
extending vocabulary by adding prefixes and suffixes to base words

AC9E3LA11.minimum_width: Correctly form three contractions using apostrophes; correctly form singular possession with an apostrophe in at least two examples.
AC9E3LA11.typical_width: Use apostrophes for contractions (signalling missing letters) and for singular and plural possession across a range of contexts; apply correctly in own writing.
wider: Investigate why 'won't' doesn't follow the expected contraction pattern, and explore other irregular contractions

Limited width: apostrophe conventions are precision rules that do not vary significantly across contexts at this year band. Extension goes toward harder possession cases (irregular plurals) and contextual appropriateness of contractions.
elaborations: using apostrophes to create contractions; for example, 'do not' – 'don't', 'will not' – 'won't'
using apostrophes to show singular possession; for example, 'my friend's book'
using apostrophes to show plural possession; for example, 'the bees' hive'

AC9E3LE01.minimum_width: Compare two versions of the same story type and identify at least two differences in how characters, events or settings are presented.
AC9E3LE01.typical_width: Explore how different authors tell the same story with variations in character, event and setting; discuss how the same character type (e.g. the wolf) is portrayed differently; explore how Australian settings are portrayed in stories.
wider: Compare a traditional story told by a First Nations Australian author with a mainstream version, discussing what reflects different relationships with Country, family and community
Discuss why different authors might portray the same character type differently, connecting authorial choice to cultural perspective and purpose
elaborations: exploring the ways wide-ranging authors tell the same story, identifying variations in the use of characters, settings and events
discussing characters and their relationship with Country/Place and families in literature by First Nations Australian authors
discussing similarities and differences in the way the wolf is portrayed in different versions of traditional stories
exploring the ways Australian settings are portrayed in stories

AC9E3LE02.minimum_width: Identify one connection between a character's experience and a personal experience, and explain how the connection helps understanding; state a preference for a text and give a reason connected to personal experience.
AC9E3LE02.typical_width: Draw on prior knowledge and personal experience to make meaningful connections to characters in texts; select and discuss favourite texts explaining reasons that connect to what the text made them feel or reminded them of.
wider: Compare connections made by different students to the same character, discussing how different experiences lead to different connections
Revisit a text that wasn't initially a favourite after a new personal experience, and discuss whether the connection changed
elaborations: discussing relevant prior knowledge and past experiences to make meaningful connections to characters in texts
selecting and discussing favourite texts and explaining reasons for preferences

AC9E3LE03.minimum_width: Identify two descriptive language choices that portray a character or setting; identify the mood of a text and one choice that creates it.
AC9E3LE03.typical_width: Identify and discuss how descriptive language creates setting and portrays character traits; discuss how language and illustrations work together to create mood in texts.
wider: Compare how the same character is described at different points in the story and discuss how language changes as the character develops
Find a text where the illustration creates a different or ironic mood from the written language, and discuss the effect of the contrast
elaborations: identifying and discussing how the use of descriptive language creates setting and influences mood
discussing the language used to describe the traits of characters in stories, their actions, speech and relationships with others

AC9E3LE04.minimum_width: Identify one piece of imagery and one sound device in texts, and discuss one effect that each creates.
AC9E3LE04.typical_width: Discuss the effects of imagery in texts — including natural and sensory imagery; identify and discuss the effects of sound devices including onomatopoeia, alliteration and rhyme; generate questions about why authors made device choices.
wider: Compare imagery used to describe the same natural phenomenon in two texts and discuss how different choices create different effects
Explore how imagery in a First Nations Australian text conveys relationship with Country/Place that goes beyond description
elaborations: discussing the effects of imagery in texts; for example, the use of imagery related to nature
generating questions to discuss effects; for example, 'Why does the poet use onomatopoeia here?'

AC9E3LE05.minimum_width: Create a short imaginative text that adapts at least one element from a read text and uses at least one literary language feature deliberately.
AC9E3LE05.typical_width: Draw on literary texts for inspiration — adapting settings, changing endings, building on characters; use language features from studied texts including descriptive language, dialogue and imagery in own imaginative writing.
wider: Adapt a traditional story by shifting the setting to a familiar Australian or local context and discuss how the story changes
Experiment with using literary devices discussed in LE04 deliberately in a creative text, explaining why each was chosen
elaborations: drawing on literary texts read, viewed and listened to for inspiration and ideas to create imaginative texts
adapting texts read, viewed and listened to by changing the setting or revising an ending
discussing characters encountered in literary texts and sharing ideas about how those characters might behave in new situations

AC9E3LY01.minimum_width: Compare two texts with the same purpose but different audiences and identify at least two ways they differ because of the audience.
AC9E3LY01.typical_width: Identify how texts with the same purpose differ for different audiences — examining vocabulary, image choices, examples and complexity as audience-driven choices across safety, instruction and persuasive contexts.
wider: Compare instructions for assembling the same item for different age groups, discussing what specific changes are made to suit each audience
Find similar-purpose texts aimed at children versus adults and evaluate whether the audience-related choices are effective
elaborations: identifying the ways in which a safety campaign varies depending on its audience; for example, a safety campaign for young children compared with one for older children or adults
identifying how the instructions for assembling and using toys vary according to the age of the child

AC9E3LY02.minimum_width: Make one contribution in a discussion that builds on a previous speaker's idea; demonstrate adjusting language for two different audiences.
AC9E3LY02.typical_width: Build on and connect to others' ideas; listen actively for specific information; use language appropriately across different group contexts; contribute to group roles including different speaking and listening functions.
wider: Practice specific group roles (chairperson, recorder, reporter) and discuss how each role requires different interaction skills
Compare language used in a formal group discussion versus casual conversation, practising adjustment between contexts
elaborations: building on and connecting ideas and opinions expressed by others
listening actively, including listening for specific information
learning the specific speaking or listening skills of different group roles
using language appropriately in different situations; for example, explaining a procedure to peers versus to the teacher

AC9E3LY03.minimum_width: Identify the audience and purpose of two different text types with evidence; identify one language feature designed to engage or influence the target audience and explain how.
AC9E3LY03.typical_width: Identify audience and purpose of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts; identify words, phrases and images intended to persuade; discuss how language features engage and influence the intended audience.
wider: Examine features of advertisements specifically targeting children and discuss how language choices exploit what children find appealing or trustworthy
Compare how an imaginative text engages its audience differently from a persuasive text, identifying what different types of engagement look like
elaborations: identifying words, phrases and images intended to persuade listeners, viewers or readers
identifying features of advertisements that target children
identifying the purpose of an imaginative text

AC9E3LY04.minimum_width: Demonstrate using at least two knowledge sources (phonic + semantic or grammatical) to decode an unknown word; demonstrate self-correction when meaning breaks down.
AC9E3LY04.typical_width: Use phonic, vocabulary and grammatical knowledge together to read unknown words; read a wider range of texts from different learning areas including chapter books; monitor and self-correct to maintain meaning.
wider: Compare decoding strategies used for an unfamiliar proper noun versus an unfamiliar content word — discussing which knowledge sources are most useful for each
Reflect on which decoding strategies work best across different subject-area texts
elaborations: using phonic knowledge, word knowledge, vocabulary and grammatical knowledge to read unknown words
reading a wider range of texts from different learning areas, including chapter books

AC9E3LY05.minimum_width: Apply at least two comprehension strategies to build meaning from a text; make one evaluative judgement about a text (relevant/important) with a reason.
AC9E3LY05.typical_width: Use comprehension strategies including prediction, inference and questioning to build literal and inferred meaning; compare how different texts present similar ideas; determine relevance for a task; evaluate information and ideas.
wider: Compare two texts that present different information about the same topic and discuss how to decide which is more reliable
Evaluate which source (book, video, website) is most useful for a specific research purpose and justify the choice
elaborations: making predictions about a text
determining important ideas, events or details in texts
comparing and contrasting how different texts present similar ideas or information
drawing inferences, using evidence from the text and prior knowledge
determining the relevance of a text for a particular task

AC9E3LY06.minimum_width: Plan a text with gathered ideas and a selected structure; create a text with topic-specific vocabulary and compound sentences; edit for at least one accuracy and one content issue.
AC9E3LY06.typical_width: Plan by gathering ideas and selecting appropriate text structure; create using simple and compound sentences and topic-specific vocabulary; edit with dictionaries, spellcheck and apostrophe checks; publish using digital tools.
wider: Compare planning strategies for an imaginative versus an informative text — discussing what changes and what stays the same
Develop a personal editing checklist based on known error patterns and apply it to a draft
elaborations: gathering information and ideas about a topic in preparation for writing
selecting appropriate text structure for a writing purpose, and sequencing content for clarity
using appropriate simple and compound sentences to express and combine ideas
using vocabulary, including topic-specific vocabulary, relevant to the type of text and purpose
using digital tools to plan, sequence, compose and edit texts
checking for correct use of apostrophes for contractions and to indicate possession

AC9E3LY07.minimum_width: Research a topic, plan using a storyboard or list, and deliver a presentation with at least one deliberate tone or pace adjustment.
AC9E3LY07.typical_width: Research a topic to prepare an oral or multimodal presentation; plan the sequence using storyboards; explain ideas to a peer when planning; adjust tone and pace to purpose and audience in delivery.
wider: Compare how planning a multimodal presentation differs from an oral-only one — discussing what additional decisions are needed
Record and review a presentation delivery, identifying one moment where tone or pace could be improved and why
elaborations: researching a topic to prepare an oral or multimodal presentation
planning the sequence of ideas and information using techniques such as storyboards
adjusting tone and pace to purpose and audience
explaining ideas to a peer when planning a presentation

AC9E3LY08.minimum_width: Write a set of words using joined letters with clearly formed letters and consistent size.
AC9E3LY08.typical_width: Write words and sentences using joined letters that are clearly formed and consistent in size across extended writing tasks.
wider: Compare joined and unjoined writing of the same text and discuss how consistency of size and joining affects readability
Limited width: handwriting is a motor skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Extension is additional practice with joins that are individually difficult.

AC9E3LY09.minimum_width: Read and write four multisyllabic words with complex consonant patterns correctly, explaining the sound each pattern represents.
AC9E3LY09.typical_width: Apply phoneme-grapheme knowledge to read and write words with consonant digraphs and blends including digraphs representing different sounds; use blending and segmenting across syllable boundaries.
wider: Collect examples of the same digraph representing different sounds and sort them, developing a generalisation about when each pronunciation applies
Apply syllable-splitting to decode unfamiliar long words encountered in subject-area reading
elaborations: reading and writing more complex words with consonant digraphs and consonant blends
reading and writing consonant digraphs representing different sounds; for example, 'machine' and 'chef'

AC9E3LY10.minimum_width: Identify the base word and prefix in three multimorphemic words and explain how the prefix changes meaning; correctly apply the doubling or 'drop e' rule when adding a suffix.
AC9E3LY10.typical_width: Use prefixes to change base word meanings; apply generalisations for adding suffixes including doubling the final consonant and dropping 'e'; read and comprehend new multimorphemic words using morphological knowledge.
wider: Collect words with the same prefix and generalise about what it consistently does to meaning
Limited width: suffix generalisations are precision spelling rules at this year band. Extension goes toward harder cases (irregular forms, exceptions) rather than significant contextual widening.
elaborations: understanding how to use knowledge of prefixes to change the meaning of a base word
using generalisations for adding a suffix to a base word to form a plural or past tense

AC9E3LY11.minimum_width: Correctly spell four words with less common patterns after short vowels; read and write four words with 3-letter blends.
AC9E3LY11.typical_width: Use phonic knowledge to explore and apply less common letter patterns after short vowels (e.g. 'tch', 'dge') and 3-letter consonant blends in reading and writing.
wider: Collect words with 'tch' and 'ch' after a short vowel and explore when each is used — developing a generalisation

Limited width: less common letter patterns are primarily a spelling memorisation and pattern recognition task at this year band. Extension goes toward identifying more unusual patterns rather than contextual widening.
elaborations: using phonic knowledge to explore less common letter patterns after short vowels; for example, 'tch' and 'dge'
using phonic knowledge and knowledge of letter patterns to spell words with 3-letter blends

AC9E3LY12.minimum_width: Read and write 20 high-frequency words automatically; correctly select and spell the right homophone in three sentence contexts.
AC9E3LY12.typical_width: Recognise and write most high-frequency words automatically; use context and syntactic knowledge to correctly select and spell common homophones.
wider: Identify which high-frequency words are still causing errors in personal writing and develop a targeted learning strategy for those specific words

Limited width: high-frequency word recognition and homophone selection are largely memorisation tasks at this year band. Extension goes toward less common homophones and reflection on personal error patterns.
elaborations: using context and syntactic knowledge to spell homophones; for example, 'break' or 'brake'
